title: Selective, durable control of pathological chronic pain

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a mechanism-specific treatment that durably controls pathological chronic pain while preserving protective nociception: the ability to detect potentially damaging events and respond to them. The intended benefit is relief substantial enough to improve daily life, sustained for as long as treatment is needed, without escalating doses, addiction, or disabling central-nervous-system effects. This is a target capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

The defining distinction is between suppressing an ongoing pathological pain state and retaining useful warning sensation. A treatment could relieve pain yet fall short if it also prevented patients from recognizing new injuries, lost effectiveness over time, or caused unacceptable impairment. Conversely, successful pain control would not necessarily repair the disease or tissue damage producing the pain. These distinctions define the proposed capability independently of any particular drug or delivery method.

Peripheral sodium-channel targeting provides a demonstrated component of pain treatment: the FDA documented acute postoperative pain relief with oral suzetrigine. That achievement establishes acute analgesic efficacy in the studied settings, but the supplied release does not demonstrate the combination of chronic relief, preserved protective sensation, and long-term tolerability required here.

significance.text: As a conditional clinical judgment, combining durable relief with preserved warning sensation would substantially change chronic pain treatment. The direct consequence would be control of spontaneous pain and its interference with daily life in patients for whom efficacy was demonstrated. Sustained benefit without dose escalation or disabling central effects would make continued treatment more useful, rather than merely producing a short period of analgesia.

Reduced opioid-related harm is a plausible downstream benefit to the extent that an effective treatment replaces opioid exposure. It is not an automatic consequence of introducing another analgesic: the effect would depend on prescribing, uptake, and actual substitution. The FDA release identifies an opportunity for a new non-opioid acute-pain treatment to mitigate some opioid-associated risks, but does not establish that outcome for durable chronic-pain treatment.

The scope of the proposed advance is pain control, not repair of an injured nerve, damaged joint, cancer, or other underlying cause. Improved activity or rehabilitation would be conditional downstream possibilities, not guaranteed restoration of tissue or function. The supplied evidence also does not substantiate broad claims that existing chronic-pain drugs generally provide only partial relief, impair thinking, cause dependence, or lose effectiveness; those comparisons require treatment-specific evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability within this record is selective, sustained control of pathological chronic pain in people. The supplied evidence demonstrates acute postoperative analgesia, but does not show that pathological chronic pain can be suppressed while protective nociception remains intact over continued treatment. This is a boundary of the supplied evidence, not proof that no intervention anywhere has achieved the capability.

Scientific and engineering synthesis: the central challenge is to identify and control a mechanism sustaining the pathological pain state with sufficient selectivity to spare useful warning signals. A mechanism-specific intervention must do more than engage a pain-related target: its effects must separate the unwanted persistent state from protective responses in patients. The supplied material does not establish that this separation is technically feasible, identify a validated mechanism that accomplishes it, or show how broadly such a mechanism would apply across chronic-pain conditions.

Further proposed barriers concern durability, safety, and measurement. Continued treatment must retain clinically meaningful benefit without requiring progressive dose increases, and must avoid unacceptable dependence, misuse, respiratory depression, or central impairment. Clinical evaluation must distinguish pain relief from sedation or reduced activity, assess protective sensation directly, and determine whether benefit extends beyond one selected condition. Acute efficacy alone cannot resolve these requirements.

current_state.text: On 30 January 2025, the FDA approved Journavx (suzetrigine) 50-milligram oral tablets, described as a first-in-class non-opioid analgesic, for moderate to severe acute pain in adults. The release describes targeting sodium channels in the peripheral nervous system. Although the earlier research identifies suzetrigine as a NaV1.8 inhibitor, the supplied FDA release does not identify the channel subtype, so that specificity is not treated as verified by this record.

Two randomized trials evaluated pain after abdominoplasty and after bunionectomy. Both showed statistically significant pain reduction compared with placebo. Participants whose pain control was inadequate could use ibuprofen as rescue medication. These findings support acute postoperative efficacy under the studied conditions; the supplied review does not establish a numerical effect size or superiority over existing non-opioid chronic-pain care.

FDA described safety data from 874 participants in the controlled surgical trials, with supportive data from 256 participants in an open-label study involving varied acute-pain conditions. These are safety-study participant counts, not evidence of long-term chronic-pain efficacy or of preserved protective nociception. The acute-pain indication and these studies do not establish freedom from tolerance, dependence, or other risks during prolonged treatment.

The supplied review reports that the FDA release was available in full, with no indicated truncation or extraction problems. Its retrieval on 1 November 2026 does not update its January 2025 content. No peer-reviewed chronic-pain trial, successor-treatment evidence, or documented search covering subsequent developments was supplied. The record therefore establishes the historical acute-pain advance but cannot determine the broader state of selective chronic-pain control as of November 2026. Missing evidence here does not show that later results are false or nonexistent.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: randomized trials in at least two common chronic-pain states, such as painful diabetic neuropathy and chronic neuropathic low-back or radicular pain, would show large, durable reductions in spontaneous pain and interference with daily life. Each trial would specify an appropriate existing non-opioid care comparator and demonstrate superiority on prespecified clinically meaningful outcomes. These are proposed criteria, not established authoritative standards; no particular pain-scale point reduction is adopted as a universal cutoff.
completion_criteria.label: Superior pain relief and functioning in two chronic-pain states

completion_criteria.text: Durability would require a prespecified follow-up period appropriate to continued chronic-pain treatment, together with reporting of dose changes, treatment discontinuation, and persistence of functional benefit. Protective nociception would need direct assessment rather than inference from pain scores alone. Relief confined to the first days after surgery would not satisfy the proposal. The supplied evidence does not justify a particular minimum duration or a specific protective-sensation testing protocol.
completion_criteria.label: Durable functional benefit and protective nociception are directly assessed

completion_criteria.text: Trials and subsequent follow-up would monitor tolerance, dependence, misuse, respiratory depression, disabling central effects, and clinically relevant consequences of impaired warning sensation. An absence of detected events would need interpretation against sample size, exposure duration, and ascertainment methods; it would not establish zero risk. Reproducible results across independent studies would strengthen the case, with transparent reporting of nonresponders, adverse effects, and populations excluded from testing.
completion_criteria.label: Safety risks are monitored and interpreted against trial exposure

completion_criteria.text: Success would establish the capability within the tested indications, patient groups, doses, and treatment durations. Two positive indications would demonstrate useful breadth across those conditions, not universal efficacy for all chronic pain. Practical boundaries would include whether patients can sustain treatment, whether benefit remains meaningful during ordinary daily activity, and whether underlying disease still requires separate treatment.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated capability stays within tested indications and treatment conditions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: CLM-04, Restoration of adult human central nervous system circuitry after injury, overlaps through neural function and injury-related symptoms. Its defining goal is restoration of circuitry, whereas CLM-12 concerns selective control of pathological pain and could succeed without rebuilding damaged circuitry. CLM-03, Arrest and recovery of function in symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease, likewise targets disease arrest and functional recovery; a neurological treatment setting alone does not make it the same capability.

Roster-based synthesis: CLM-01, Programmable antigen-specific immune tolerance, and CLM-09, Curative in vivo genome writing beyond the liver, describe distinct biological capabilities that could conceivably contribute to a future pain intervention. That possibility is conceptual, not established by the supplied evidence. CLM-12 does not require immune tolerance or genome writing, and achieving either of those capabilities would not itself demonstrate selective, durable pain control.

Roster-based synthesis: CLM-07, Reproducible eradication of metastatic carcinoma, illustrates the distinction between controlling pain and removing its cause. Relief of cancer-related pain would not establish carcinoma eradication, while cancer eradication would require its own disease-specific evidence. Similarly, CLM-06, Therapeutic remuscularization of the adult human heart, and CLM-15, Restoration of nephron number in the adult human kidney, concern tissue restoration that pain relief alone cannot demonstrate.

Roster-based synthesis: CLM-08, Safe multi-tissue reversal of human biological aging, could share downstream goals involving function and quality of life, but has a different biological endpoint. Chronic-pain improvement would not by itself demonstrate reversal of aging. The remaining roster entries address infection clearance or prevention, transplantation and organ construction, cancer screening, or blood replacement; no specific mechanistic overlap with selective chronic-pain control is established in the supplied material.

change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent despite limitations in evidence for individual supporting assertions.

change_log.change: Replaced field-wide assertions that the capability has not been achieved with a bounded account of what the supplied evidence demonstrates.
change_log.reason: One acute-pain release and an empty freshness record cannot establish the absence of qualifying chronic-pain results across the field.

change_log.change: Retained the January 2025 approval, oral formulation, adult acute-pain indication, surgical settings, placebo superiority, rescue ibuprofen, and separate safety counts.
change_log.reason: The supplied review confirms these historical details and their scope.

change_log.reason: The reviewed FDA release describes peripheral sodium-channel targeting but does not name the subtype.

change_log.change: Qualified broad comparisons with existing chronic-pain drugs and made opioid-harm reduction conditional on replacement of opioid exposure.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not substantiate the general treatment comparisons or establish downstream harm reduction in chronic pain.

change_log.change: Integrated the distinction between pain control, preserved warning sensation, and repair of underlying disease throughout the relevant sections.
change_log.reason: These are separate clinical outcomes, and acute analgesia or symptom relief cannot substitute for demonstrating the others.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration to include comparator selection, follow-up, direct protective-sensation assessment, reproducibility, and interpretation of safety signals.
change_log.reason: Convincing evaluation requires operational definitions and cannot infer absence of risk from an absence of observed events.

change_log.change: Preserved the two-indication proposal while limiting its inference to demonstrated breadth.
change_log.reason: Finite trials cannot establish efficacy across every chronic-pain condition or patient population.

change_log.change: Separated conceptual synthesis and proposed evaluation requirements from sourced historical findings.
change_log.reason: The FDA release does not substantiate the full chronic-pain goal, its technical feasibility, or the proposed completion criteria.

change_log.change: Added roster-based overlap and distinctions without merging concepts.
change_log.reason: Related mechanisms, symptom benefits, and disease-repair goals do not make the roster entries interchangeable.

unresolved_issues: No documented search covering subsequent developments was supplied, so the state of the broader capability through November 2026 remains undetermined.
The NaV1.8 subtype identification in the earlier research remains unverified by the supplied source; omission from this release is not evidence that the identification is false.
The supplied material does not establish a mechanism that separates pathological chronic pain from protective nociception in people or determine how broadly such selectivity could apply.

No supplied chronic-pain trial establishes sustained benefit, preserved protective sensation, or long-term avoidance of tolerance, dependence, misuse, respiratory depression, and disabling central effects.
Comparator regimens, clinically meaningful benefit thresholds, follow-up duration, protective-nociception measures, and safety-study size remain to be specified for the proposed demonstrations.
Broad claims about the shortcomings of existing chronic-pain treatments require additional treatment-specific evidence.
No substantive review recommendation was rejected; operational details that the review identified as necessary remain explicitly unresolved.

brief.title: Lasting pain relief that keeps injury warnings intact
possible: People with persistent pain could get lasting relief while still feeling the warning pain of a new injury. Treatment would target the process sustaining their pain, remain effective without rising doses, and avoid addiction or disabling effects on thinking and alertness.
why: Pain would interfere less with daily life, and continued treatment would keep helping people function. Preserving warning pain would let them recognize new injuries while controlling the pain that persists.

sources.showed: Suzetrigine reduced short-term pain after surgery compared with placebo, a dummy treatment. It targets sodium channels, proteins that help nerves carry pain signals outside the brain and spinal cord.
sources.quote: Both trials demonstrated a statistically significant superior reduction in pain with Journavx compared to placebo.
sources.cited_for: Targeting pain signals outside the brain can provide pain relief after surgery.
sources.not_established: Short-term surgical pain relief does not establish lasting chronic-pain control or preserved injury warnings.

sources.showed: An implanted device delivering electrical pulses to the spinal cord provided pain relief lasting 24 months in patients with diabetes-related nerve pain. Sleep and quality of life also improved.
sources.quote: Furthermore, the majority of participants demonstrated neurological improvement.
sources.cited_for: Spinal cord stimulation can provide sustained relief in a selected chronic-pain condition.
sources.not_established: Improved nerve examinations do not establish that patients reliably retain injury-warning pain during everyday life.

sources.showed: An earlier report from the same trial found better pain relief with spinal cord stimulation plus usual care than with usual care alone. Patients knew which treatment they received.
sources.quote: there was a significant benefit of 10-kHz spinal cord stimulation
sources.cited_for: The trial supports pain relief without worsening existing nerve problems in diabetes-related nerve pain.
sources.not_established: This report does not establish lasting selective pain control across different chronic-pain conditions.

sources.showed: A conference abstract reported reduced diabetes-related nerve pain during 12 weeks of suzetrigine treatment. It reported no serious adverse events, meaning medical problems during treatment, linked to the drug.
sources.quote: there were no serious AEs related to suzetrigine.
sources.cited_for: Suzetrigine has shown an early clinical signal of benefit for chronic nerve pain.
sources.not_established: The abstract does not establish superiority over existing care, preserved warning sensation, or long-term safety.

shown: Petersen and colleagues reported the longest-lasting chronic-pain benefit among these studies: spinal cord stimulation relieved diabetes-related nerve pain for 24 months, with improved sleep and nerve examinations. Patients knew their treatment, and the longer follow-up included people who switched from usual care.

Suzetrigine has demonstrated pain relief after surgery and early benefit in diabetes-related nerve pain. Neither approach yet establishes the full combination of lasting chronic-pain relief, preserved injury warnings, and acceptable long-term risks.
missing: Trials must establish substantial, lasting pain relief and better daily functioning across different chronic-pain conditions.
Direct testing must establish that patients retain useful injury-warning pain during continued treatment.
Long-term follow-up must establish sustained benefit without rising doses, addiction, or disabling effects on alertness.

milestones.label: Better pain relief and functioning in two chronic-pain conditions
milestones.explanation: Randomized trials in two common chronic-pain conditions would have to beat appropriate existing non-opioid care on meaningful pain relief and daily functioning. This would establish useful benefit across conditions.

milestones.label: Lasting daily benefit with injury warnings preserved
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would have to track lasting functional benefit, dose changes, treatment stopping, and direct tests of injury-warning sensation. This would distinguish sustained selective relief from temporary pain suppression.

milestones.label: Safety risks measured over continued treatment
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to monitor fading benefit, dependence, misuse, slowed breathing, disabling brain effects, and harm from missed warnings. Their size and duration would determine how much reassurance absent events provide.

milestones.label: Useful treatment within clearly tested limits
milestones.explanation: Results would have to establish benefit during ordinary activity within tested conditions, patient groups, doses, and durations. This would define who can sustain useful treatment while underlying disease receives separate care.

uncertain: Can treatment separate persistent pathological pain from useful injury warnings, and how widely could that separation work?
What benefit threshold, follow-up period, and warning-sensation tests would adequately demonstrate success?
How much treatment exposure would reveal uncommon harms and loss of effectiveness?

page.title: Chronic pain relief with preserved protective nociception
page.definition: A treatment targeting a defined pain mechanism relieves pain that has persisted or recurred for more than 3 months. The person remains able to detect and avoid a new injury because nociception, the nervous system’s encoding of potentially damaging stimuli, is preserved. Relief and improved function last during treatment without progressive dose increases, addiction, clinically important dependence or disabling impairment. The 8% capsaicin patch already treats some neuropathic pain, but can temporarily reduce sensitivity to harmful stimuli.

goal.need: In 2023, chronic pain limited life or work on most days or every day for 8.5% of US adults. About one in five US adults with chronic pain are prescribed opioids. Lasting relief could help people resume daily activities and reduce their need for opioids while preserving the warning that lets them act on a new injury. For someone with diabetic neuropathy, that warning can be the pain of a cut or blister. Existing sensory loss still makes daily foot checks necessary.

figures.caption: Chronic pain among US adults in 2023
figures.note: Adults aged 18 years and older in the civilian noninstitutionalized population. Chronic pain means pain on most days or every day during the preceding 3 months; high-impact chronic pain additionally limits life or work that frequently.

completion.title: A treatment controls chronic pain for at least 6 months while preserving protective nociception.
completion.criterion: For one specified chronic-pain indication, controlled human evidence establishes maintained pain relief and functional improvement after at least 6 months, together with retained injury-warning sensation and avoidance responses on direct tests during treatment. Benefit persists at a maintained dose without addiction, clinically important dependence or disabling impairment. The prospective protocol must specify sensory preservation margins, efficacy endpoints, harm limits and follow-up. This provisional composite has no externally endorsed sensory preservation margin.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; provisional synthesis because no outside body located defines the combined capability.
completion.basis: FDA and EMA analgesic-development guidance, ICH E1, NIH HEAL priorities, IASP terminology and IMMPACT recommendations were searched for a joint durability and protective-nociception test; none was found. The six-month component follows EMA's maintenance-of-efficacy design. Sensory preservation remains a proposed requirement without a published universal pass/fail margin.

milestones.title: A drug candidate shows target-linked activity in vitro and in vivo with properties suited to clinical use.
milestones.criterion: Identify a small molecule or biologic and provide evidence linking its target to the proposed pain indication. Show biological activity in vitro and in vivo and demonstrate absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity properties appropriate for the intended clinical use.
milestones.set_by: NIH HEAL Initiative, RFA-NS-21-010, General Entry Criteria; these criteria concern small molecules and biologics.
milestones.threshold_quote: the proposed therapeutic must have in vitro and in vivo biological activity and ADMET properties appropriate for the intended clinical use.

milestones.title: A phase 1 study characterizes human drug exposure, dose tolerance and acute adverse effects.
milestones.criterion: Administer the candidate drug to healthy volunteers or patients under a phase 1 protocol. Characterize exposure and assess how much drug participants tolerate and which acute adverse effects occur.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Step 3: Clinical Research, description of phase 1 drug studies.
milestones.threshold_quote: how much of a drug the body can tolerate and what its acute side effects are.

milestones.title: Weekly mean diabetic neuropathic pain falls from baseline within a dose group at week 12.
milestones.criterion: In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, calculate the change from baseline to week 12 in the weekly average of daily pain intensity on a 0–10 scale. Estimate the mean change within each VX-548 dose group and report its 95% confidence interval. A decrease is a within-group signal. This analysis does not estimate superiority to pregabalin or placebo.
milestones.set_by: Vertex Pharmaceuticals, protocol VX21-548-103, version 3.0, dated 17 February 2023, registered as NCT05660538; this endpoint was written for painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
milestones.threshold_quote: The primary analysis will be a within-group comparison in any VX-548 dose group.

milestones.title: Diabetic neuropathic pain falls ≥50% at 3 months without meaningful neurological worsening.
milestones.criterion: Count a participant as a responder if lower-limb pain falls at least 50% from baseline on a 10 cm visual analogue scale and the neurological examination shows no meaningful worsening of baseline deficits at 3 months. Compare responder proportions for 10 kHz spinal cord stimulation plus conventional medical management versus medical management alone at a two-sided significance level of 0.05.
milestones.set_by: Nevro and SENZA-PDN investigators, prespecified primary endpoint of NCT03228420, reproduced in the primary publication; written for painful diabetic neuropathy.
milestones.threshold_quote: participants with 50% pain relief or more on VAS without worsening of baseline neurological deficits at 3 months.

milestones.title: A chronic-pain drug has 100 patients treated for 1 year and 300–600 treated for 6 months.
milestones.criterion: For a drug intended for chronic or repeated intermittent use beyond 6 months in a non-life-threatening condition, ICH generally anticipates about 1,500 people exposed overall. Usually 300–600 patients treated for 6 months and 100 treated for at least 1 year at intended clinical doses are adequate for assessing longer-term adverse events. The guideline allows exceptions according to the drug, indication and safety findings.
milestones.set_by: International Conference on Harmonisation, E1, paragraphs 4–7; a drug-specific exposure benchmark for long-term treatment of non-life-threatening conditions.
milestones.threshold_quote: 100 patients exposed for a minimum of one-year is considered to be acceptable to include as part of the safety data base.

milestones.title: A drug retains analgesic efficacy on randomized withdrawal after ≥6 months of stable treatment.
milestones.criterion: After at least 6 months of stable open-label treatment, randomize responders to continued drug or placebo. Demonstrate maintenance by comparing time to prespecified symptom relapse or the proportion relapsing by a prespecified time. Characterize tolerance by assessing whether maintaining the response requires increasing doses. EMA also accepts adequately justified alternative designs.
milestones.set_by: EMA Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, analgesic-development guideline, section 5.2.5; this is a drug-specific maintenance-of-efficacy design.
milestones.threshold_quote: Following stable open label treatment for at least 6 months, patients are randomised to receive either active or placebo.

milestones.title: Targeting a pain mechanism reduces nerve-injury hypersensitivity while sparing acute withdrawal in mice.
milestones.criterion: Compare withdrawal responses to mechanical or thermal stimulation after nerve injury with responses in matched controls. The intervention must attenuate injury-induced hypersensitivity while leaving the acute response to stimulation detectable at control thresholds or latencies in uninjured mice. Report each stimulus and response separately.
milestones.set_by: Paired behavioral tests in mouse models of nerve injury, as used by Malmberg and colleagues and by Torres-Rodriguez and colleagues. The comparisons are specific to the stimuli tested.
milestones.threshold_quote: reverses nerve injury-induced hypersensitivity without affecting baseline nociception.

milestones.title: A controlled drug trial demonstrates sustained chronic-pain relief for at least 12 weeks after titration.
milestones.criterion: For the specified chronic-pain indication, demonstrate sustained efficacy against a control on a prespecified pain measure validated for that condition. EMA generally recommends a randomized parallel-group pivotal trial with at least 12 weeks of treatment excluding titration. An alternative design requires justification.
milestones.set_by: EMA Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use, guideline on the clinical development of medicinal products intended for the treatment of pain, section 6.2.5.
milestones.threshold_quote: a treatment period of at least 12 weeks

milestones.title: Blinded examiners assess changes in sharp and thermal sensation over 52 weeks in diabetic neuropathy.
milestones.criterion: In painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, compare repeat 8% capsaicin patch treatment plus standard care with standard care alone. Examiners blinded to treatment test both feet at baseline and study end. Rate warm, cold and sharp stimuli at five sites per foot as absent, diminished, normal or painful. Report the proportions whose ratings improve, remain stable or worsen. This endpoint measures sensory change without specifying a margin for preserved injury avoidance.
milestones.set_by: PACE investigators, secondary sensory assessment in NCT01478607, described in the primary 52-week safety publication.
milestones.threshold_quote: ‘Bedside’ sensory and reflex testing was performed on both feet at baseline and EoS to identify any clinically relevant deficits in sensory function.

not_found: No outside document located defined a combined completion test for maintained chronic-pain relief, preserved protective nociception, dose stability and freedom from clinically important dependence or impairment.
No externally endorsed clinical margin for preservation of injury-warning sensation during continued chronic-pain treatment was located.
ClinicalTrials.gov study pages returned no readable study details; the diabetic-neuropathy phase 2 protocol was accessible separately.
No statement from IASP, NIH, FDA or EMA was found disputing the value or feasibility of preserving protective nociception during chronic-pain relief.

results.finding: In 216 randomized adults with painful diabetic neuropathy, the 3-month NNT for at least 50% pain relief with spinal cord stimulation plus usual care was 1.2.
results.detail: The sample size is the total randomized. The excerpt gives no 3-month analysis denominator for the pain-only NNT.
results.quote:
the SENZA-PDN study had very low 
NNT values for ≥50% pain relief versus CMM alone at 1, 3, and 6 
months, with values of 1.4, 1.2, and 1.3, respectively.

results.finding: In refractory painful diabetic neuropathy (216 randomized, 189 analyzed), 10-kHz spinal cord stimulation plus medical management increased 3-month composite response by 73.6 percentage points.
results.detail: The primary analysis included randomized patients with known endpoint status. It counted temporary stimulation failures and withdrawals due to adverse events in the stimulation arm as nonresponders.
results.quote:
The primary end
point assessed in the intention-to-treat population was met by 5 of 94 patients in the CMM
group (5%) and 75 of 95 patients in the 10-kHz SCS plus CMM group (79%; difference, 73.6%;
95% CI, 64.2-83.0;P < .001).

results.finding: In a phase 2 trial of 192 adults with painful diabetic neuropathy, high-dose suzetrigine lowered the weekly mean pain score by 2.26 points from baseline at week 12.
results.detail: The sample size is total trial enrollment across the three suzetrigine groups and the pregabalin reference group.

results.finding: In a phase 2 trial of 192 adults with painful diabetic neuropathy, mean pain reductions from baseline in all suzetrigine groups persisted through week 12.
results.quote: All suzetrigine dose groups had sustained mean reductions in pain from baseline starting at Wk1; pain continued to decrease until Wk5, which was maintained through Wk12.

results.finding: Oral LX9211 inhibited established mechanical allodynia by >50% in streptozotocin-treated rats (n unreported).
results.detail: The lowest oral dose that achieved this inhibition was 1 mg/kg. Mean plasma exposure at the end of behavioral testing was 92.3 nM.
results.quote:
The lowest dose achieving 
>50% inhibition was 0.3 mg/kg and 1 mg/kg, respectively and was associated with average 
plasma exposures of 18.7 nM and 92.3 nM, respectively, on completion of behavioral testing.

results.finding: LX9211 nearly completely inhibited pain at 30 mg/kg in a rat model of postherpetic neuralgia (n unreported).
results.detail: The protocol gives a qualitative effect magnitude for the postherpetic neuralgia model.
results.quote:
Both single 
and multiple oral doses of 30 mg/kg LX9211 demonstrated almost complete inhibition of pain 
due to varicella-zoster virus (VZV) infection in this model.

results.finding: Healthy volunteers (n=146 across both phase 1 studies) generally tolerated single oral LX9211 doses up to 300 mg.
results.detail: The protocol gives pooled enrollment for the two ascending-dose studies. Its detailed multiple-dose summary reports one adverse-event discontinuation, while the dose rationale says there were none.
results.quote:
The results from the SAD study showed that LX9211 was generally well tolerated in healthy 
normal subjects at single doses up to 300 mg.

results.finding: In the 48-participant BG00010 sciatica trial, steady-state volume of distribution reached 94.8 L/kg in the highest IV dose cohort.
results.detail: The highest IV dose cohort included three BG00010 recipients. The study used single doses.
results.quote: Vss reached 94.8 l/kg at a dose of 800 μg/kg.

results.finding: In a phase 1 trial of 48 adults with unilateral sciatica, single IV doses of BG00010 were generally tolerated up to 800 μg/kg.
results.detail: Eligibility required at least six weeks of sciatica symptoms. Imaging evidence of nerve-root impingement was optional.
results.quote:
In this randomized Phase 1 study, single i.v. doses of BG00010 up to 800 μg/kg and single s.c.
doses at 50 μg/kg were generally well tolerated by subjects with sciatica.

results.finding: Duloxetine showed controlled efficacy through 12 weeks in painful diabetic neuropathy (N=1,139 across three trials).
results.detail: The dosing section allows a lower starting dose for 1–2 weeks. The excerpt does not establish the titration schedules in the efficacy trials.
results.quote:
The efficacy of duloxetine hydrochloride has been demonstrated in controlled clinical trials for 
up to 12 weeks in DPN and FM and up to 13 weeks in patients with CLBP and OA.

results.finding: Among 1,429 duloxetine recipients with painful diabetic neuropathy, 515 had more than 12 months of exposure.
results.quote:
Among these 
1429 patients, 881 had ≥6 months of exposure to duloxetine hydrochloride, and 515 had 
greater than 12 months of exposure.

results.finding: Vixotrigine for painful lumbosacral radiculopathy had a mean week-52 pain change of −3.50 points in 50 evaluable participants previously assigned placebo.
results.detail: Week-52 means use available observations and a baseline collected before parent-trial randomization. The extension ended early after the parent study missed its primary and secondary efficacy endpoints.

results.finding: The vixotrigine extension for painful lumbosacral radiculopathy exposed 302 participants to the drug.
results.detail: Study completion and the maximum adverse-event reporting window do not establish individual treatment duration. The study ended early.

results.finding: Vixotrigine for painful lumbosacral radiculopathy had a mean week-26 pain change of −3.13 points in 89 evaluable participants previously assigned placebo.
results.detail: All extension cohorts received vixotrigine. The protocol permitted a dose reduction for tolerability, and the registry does not report dose trajectories linked to maintained relief.

results.finding: In the VM202 diabetic neuropathy trial (safety n=103), circulating plasmid levels fell sharply or were undetectable within 1 week of dosing.
results.detail: Loss of detectable plasmid from blood does not establish its metabolic fate or route of excretion.
results.quote: Copies of VM202 in whole blood were greatly reduced or completely negative within 1 week after VM202 dosing (data not shown).

results.finding: In the VM202 diabetic neuropathy trial (safety n=103), 26 participants had grade 1 injection-site reactions.
results.detail: The trial divided the assigned dose between days 0 and 14.
results.quote: A total of 26 patients experienced Grade 1 minor injection site reactions (i.e., pain, itching, erythema, and/or bruising) with more than half (14) of the minor skin reactions occurring in the HD group.

results.finding: Low-dose VM202 recipients with painful diabetic neuropathy (n=31) had a 3.03-point mean decrease in weekly pain at day 90.
In painful diabetic neuropathy (efficacy n=84), low-dose VM202 improved diary pain versus placebo at 3 months (P=0.04).
results.detail: The subgroup taking neither gabapentin nor pregabalin showed a significant low-dose versus placebo difference at month 6. The full efficacy population did not.
results.quote: At 3 months, patients in the LD group experienced a significant reduction in pain compared to P group ( P  = 0.04) (Table 2  and Fig. 2 A).

results.finding: Among low-dose VM202 recipients with painful diabetic neuropathy (n=31), 48.4% met the day-90 diary pain response threshold.
results.detail: Neurological examinations at 6 and 9 months were separate from the day-90 responder analysis.
results.quote: At 90 days, patients in the LD group had nearly threefold more responders than Placebo ( P  = 0.06; P: 17.6% responders, LD: 48.4% responders).

results.finding: In painful diabetic neuropathy (n=156), 21.1% of below-normal mid-plantar heat tests reached normal at month 12 with repeat 8% capsaicin plus standard care.
results.detail: The percentages are calculated per test. The month-12 normalization analysis used observed data, while the end-of-study shift analysis used last observation carried forward.
results.quote: At Month 12, tests that began below normal became “normal” for heat, cold, and sharp in 21.1%, 26.4%, and 22.8% of tests, respectively.

results.finding: In painful diabetic neuropathy (77 analyzed), 93.1% receiving 10-kHz spinal cord stimulation plus usual care achieved the 3-month pain response.
results.detail: The 3-month analysis included control participants who completed follow-up and stimulation recipients who had a permanent implant and completed follow-up.
results.quote:
In the 10-kHz SCS group, 27 of 29 participants (93.1%; 95% CI, 78.0–98.1) met the pain response criterion as early as 3 months, and this response was sustained at 6 months, compared with none of the 48 CMM-alone participants (0%; 95% CI, 0.0–7.4) at 3 months (
P
< 0.001 for group difference).

results.finding: In streptozotocin-diabetic mice (n = 10), 10 mg/kg MCC950 reduced von Frey hypersensitivity versus vehicle.
results.detail: The behavioral intervention and the documented nerve fiber loss were assessed at different stages of the diabetic model.
results.quote: The treatment of NLRP3 inhibitor MCC950 alleviated the mechanical allodynia of DNP mice.

results.finding: In mice with L5 spinal nerve ligation (n=6/group), anti-CADM1 cm3E1 kept mechanical paw withdrawal thresholds elevated for 10 days.
results.detail: The authors reported unchanged contralateral von Frey thresholds without showing the data. The sham-operated group was used for gene expression measurements.
results.quote: In cm3E1-injected mice, the paw withdrawal threshold was nearly normal at 5 and 24 h, remained relatively high for 10 days, and then gradually declined at 2 and 3 weeks

results.finding: In painful diabetic neuropathy (144 analyzed), pregabalin lowered the adjusted endpoint pain score by 1.47 points versus placebo.
results.detail: DPN-131 enrolled adults with painful distal symmetrical sensorimotor polyneuropathy for at least one year. Pregabalin was given at 300 mg/day in three divided doses for 8 weeks. Somnolence and dose-related adverse-event withdrawals were documented across neuropathy trials.

results.finding: In two trials of disc-related radicular leg pain (N=518), intradiscal condoliase reduced worst leg pain versus placebo or sham at week 13.
results.detail: The trials enrolled adults with confirmed nerve root impingement. Clinical safety data included disc-related imaging changes, and Japanese postmarketing surveillance recorded serious hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis.
results.quote:
Studies 1031 and 1133 showed that condoliase reduced radicular leg pain by Week 13, 
meeting the primary endpoint with statistical significance (Figure 6) — results that were 
sustained through Week 52 (Table 20 [Study 1031]; Table 28 [Study 1133]).

results.finding: Qutenza reduced mean pain scores by 29.6% over weeks 2–8 in phase 3 study C116, which randomized 402 adults with postherpetic neuralgia.
results.detail: C116 used a low-dose capsaicin control. Human plasma exposure was low, and excretion was characterized in animals. CHMP requested long-term neurological safety follow-up. Healthy volunteers showed a transient reduction in sharp-pain detection.
results.quote:
Study C116 and C117: Following a single 60-minute Qutenza patch application a 29.6% 
reduction in pain in study C116 and 32.0% reduction in pain in study C117 was observed during 
weeks 2 to 8.

results.finding: Mirogabalin for postherpetic neuralgia (237 treated) had a median treatment duration of 365 days.
results.detail: The parent trial randomized 765 patients across placebo and mirogabalin groups for 14 weeks, and extension participants came from that trial. The parent trial therefore cannot supply the missing six-month exposures.
results.quote: Patients received treatment for mean (SD; median) of 313.4 (106.7; 365.0) days.

results.finding: In painful diabetic neuropathy (n = 824 analyzed), mirogabalin lowered average daily pain scores by 0.50 points more than placebo at the end of fixed-dose treatment.
results.detail: The efficacy result was for 30 mg/day. The 15 and 20 mg/day groups showed no statistically significant benefit on the primary endpoint.
results.quote: At week 14, the least squares mean  average daily pain score  change from baseline was −1.31, −1.34, −1.47 and −1.81, respectively, showing statistical significance for mirogabalin 30 mg/day versus placebo ( P  =   0.0027).

results.finding: In painful diabetic neuropathy (n = 703), tapentadol ER favored placebo by 1.14 points on the pain scale at week 12 after titration.
results.detail: The randomized comparison assessed maintenance of relief among patients who tolerated and responded to tapentadol ER during open-label titration. Both groups could use supplemental tapentadol ER during maintenance.
results.quote:
The mean (SD) change from baseline to week 12 of the
maintenance period was 1.28 (2.41) in the placebo group
and 0.08 (1.87) in the tapentadol ER group [LSMD for
tapentadol ER vs placebo (95 % conﬁdence interval [CI])
-1.14 ( -1.435, -0.838); P\ 0.001].

results.finding: In 163 patients with leg pain from contained lumbar disc herniation, condoliase reduced worst leg pain by 15.2 mm more than placebo at week 13.
results.detail: The week-13 comparison meets the timing target for a single-dose regimen. Eligibility requiring pain for more than 3 months and condition-specific validation of the pain measure cannot be verified from the text.
results.quote: The average changes in worst leg pain from baseline to week 13 (primary endpoint) were -49.5 mm in the condoliase group and -34.3 mm in the placebo group, and the difference of -15.2 mm was significant (95% confidence interval, -24.2 to -6.2; P = 0.001).

results.finding: Mirogabalin for postherpetic neuralgia (n=763 analyzed) lowered the week-14 average daily pain score by 0.77 points versus placebo at the highest dose.
results.quote: At week 14, the difference in average daily pain score least squares mean vs placebo was −0.41, −0.47, and −0.77, respectively; all mirogabalin groups showed statistical significance.

results.finding: In painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy (n=439 with sensory data), more than half had unchanged sensory ratings at study end.
results.quote: the majority of patients had no change from baseline to EoS

definition = "A treatment targeting a defined pain mechanism relieves pain that has persisted or recurred for more than 3 months. The person remains able to detect and avoid a new injury because nociception, the nervous system\u2019s encoding of potentially damaging stimuli, is preserved. Relief and improved function last during treatment without progressive dose increases, addiction, clinically important dependence or disabling impairment. The 8% capsaicin patch already treats some neuropathic pain, but can temporarily reduce sensitivity to harmful stimuli.". Reason: The definition leaves out the closest clinical example and uses a broader dependence exclusion than the completion criterion.

goal.need = "In 2023, chronic pain limited life or work on most days or every day for 8.5% of US adults. About one in five US adults with chronic pain are prescribed opioids. Lasting relief could help people resume daily activities and reduce their need for opioids while preserving the warning that lets them act on a new injury. For someone with diabetic neuropathy, that warning can be the pain of a cut or blister. Existing sensory loss still makes daily foot checks necessary.". Reason: The existing text points to a table without explaining what patients gain from relief that preserves injury warnings.

add statement by NINDS-funded project R01NS130044, Investigation of neural ensembles driving pain chronification, 2022: "while preserving necessary sensory discriminative processes for protective pain sensation.". Reason: The two existing statements call for more analgesic options but omit a funded project's explicit aim to preserve protective pain sensation.

add not found: "No statement from IASP, NIH, FDA or EMA was found disputing the value or feasibility of preserving protective nociception during chronic-pain relief.". Reason: The existing search notes cover thresholds but do not address institutional disagreement about the goal.
add case "Postherpetic neuralgia". Reason: Postherpetic neuralgia has a dedicated phase 2 protocol and a separate labeled indication for topical capsaicin.

add milestone after None: "Targeting a pain mechanism reduces nerve-injury hypersensitivity while sparing acute withdrawal in mice.". Reason: Target activity alone misses the early animal experiment that tests whether injury-induced hypersensitivity can be separated from acute defensive responses.

edit m1: title = "A drug candidate shows target-linked activity in vitro and in vivo with properties suited to clinical use."; criterion = "Identify a small molecule or biologic and provide evidence linking its target to the proposed pain indication. Show biological activity in vitro and in vivo and demonstrate absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity properties appropriate for the intended clinical use."; refs = [9]. Reason: The suzetrigine cell result tests only one part of the NIH candidate-entry criterion and obscures the requirements for an identified drug candidate.

edit m2: title = "A phase 1 study characterizes human drug exposure, dose tolerance and acute adverse effects."; criterion = "Administer the candidate drug to healthy volunteers or patients under a phase 1 protocol. Characterize exposure and assess how much drug participants tolerate and which acute adverse effects occur."; refs = [11]. Reason: The example dose range and study size belong to one trial and are not FDA phase 1 requirements.

edit m3: title = "Weekly mean diabetic neuropathic pain falls from baseline within a dose group at week 12."; criterion = "In adults with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, calculate the change from baseline to week 12 in the weekly average of daily pain intensity on a 0\u201310 scale. Estimate the mean change within each VX-548 dose group and report its 95% confidence interval. A decrease is a within-group signal. This analysis does not estimate superiority to pregabalin or placebo."; refs = [13]. Reason: The current wording mixes trial results and a phase 3 recruitment update with a within-group endpoint specific to painful diabetic neuropathy.

add milestone after m3: "A controlled drug trial demonstrates sustained chronic-pain relief for at least 12 weeks after titration.". Reason: The milestones omit the controlled pivotal drug trial that distinguishes sustained efficacy from improvement within a dose group.

edit m4: title = "Diabetic neuropathic pain falls \u226550% at 3 months without meaningful neurological worsening."; criterion = "Count a participant as a responder if lower-limb pain falls at least 50% from baseline on a 10 cm visual analogue scale and the neurological examination shows no meaningful worsening of baseline deficits at 3 months. Compare responder proportions for 10 kHz spinal cord stimulation plus conventional medical management versus medical management alone at a two-sided significance level of 0.05."; refs = [17]. Reason: The title omits the condition and the criterion includes observed responder counts where it should define a responder and the group comparison.

add milestone after m4: "Blinded examiners assess changes in sharp and thermal sensation over 52 weeks in diabetic neuropathy.". Reason: The neurological composite does not record which sensory modalities worsen, whereas PACE specifies blinded testing of each foot over 52 weeks.

edit m5: criterion = "For a drug intended for chronic or repeated intermittent use beyond 6 months in a non-life-threatening condition, ICH generally anticipates about 1,500 people exposed overall. Usually 300\u2013600 patients treated for 6 months and 100 treated for at least 1 year at intended clinical doses are adequate for assessing longer-term adverse events. The guideline allows exceptions according to the drug, indication and safety findings."; refs = [8]. Reason: Acute-pain approval and short-term recipient counts do not define the ICH exposure benchmark for long-term drug safety.

edit m6: title = "A drug retains analgesic efficacy on randomized withdrawal after \u22656 months of stable treatment."; criterion = "After at least 6 months of stable open-label treatment, randomize responders to continued drug or placebo. Demonstrate maintenance by comparing time to prespecified symptom relapse or the proportion relapsing by a prespecified time. Characterize tolerance by assessing whether maintaining the response requires increasing doses. EMA also accepts adequately justified alternative designs."; refs = [4]. Reason: The device follow-up is not a randomized drug-withdrawal test, and the current title omits the comparison that establishes maintenance.
structure = parallel. Reason: The device responder endpoint, sensory testing, drug-exposure database and drug-withdrawal trial answer independent questions and need not follow one another.
